prose.title: The Hawks Went Into the Auction Without a Starting Quarterback and Came Out With Two
prose.dek: Chris Klingenberg began April with no top-twelve starter on offense and no quarterback on his active roster. He nearly doubled his starting offense at the auction and still ranks last in the league, with {{f.team.0012.holes_today}} holes.

paragraphs: Quarterback is the one room that works, ranking {{f.team.0012.qb_rank|ord}}. Matthew Stafford grades Low-end QB1 and Jared Goff High-end QB2 in the superflex. That is a functional superflex pair and it took most of his auction money.

Everything else on offense is short. Receiver is the worst room in the league: Mike Evans is a Mid WR3, rookie Carnell Tate a Low-end WR3, Michael Wilson a High-end WR4 in the flex. The backfield ranks {{f.team.0012.rb_rank|ord}} on Kyren Williams at High-end RB2 and Rhamondre Stevenson at Mid RB3, with J.K. Dobbins, a Replacement-level RB, in the other flex. Travis Kelce is a Low-end TE1 and tight end ranks {{f.team.0012.te_rank|ord}}.

Behind Marcus Jones and George Karlaftis, the rest of the defense is replacement-level or rookies too new to grade. He put {{f.team.0012.idp_auction_share}} of his auction money into defenders, the smallest share of any owner, and over the previous three seasons his defenders scored the fewest points per start in the league.
Composite {{f.team.0012.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, {{f.team.0012.studs_today}} studs, {{f.team.0012.holes_today}} holes — the most in the league.

April was bleak: {{f.team.0012.holes_opening}} holes among the priced starting slots and not one top-twelve player in any of them, with {{f.team.0012.cap_opening}} committed. The quarterback slot had nobody rostered in it at all.

Three months later, at the auction lock, almost nothing had changed: {{f.team.0012.cap_preauction}} committed, holes still at {{f.team.0012.holes_opening}}, studs still at {{f.team.0012.studs_opening}}. Carnell Tate, his top rookie pick at 1.02, had replaced Michael Wilson at the second receiver slot and Wilson had moved into a flex. The quarterback slot was still empty.

Then the auction, which was the whole offseason compressed into two weeks. His starting offense nearly doubled, the second-biggest jump in the league, behind only CBP; because he started from the weakest base in the league, in total value added he ranked {{f.team.0012.faa_off_gain_rank|ord}}. Matthew Stafford filled a quarterback slot that had been vacant since April and Jared Goff took the superflex off a wide receiver. Travis Kelce replaced Dalton Kincaid at tight end. Rhamondre Stevenson took the second back slot from J.K. Dobbins.

Four priced slots improved, holes fell from {{f.team.0012.holes_opening}} to {{f.team.0012.holes_postauction}} and studs went from {{f.team.0012.studs_opening}} to {{f.team.0012.studs_postauction}}. That is real progress. It still left more holes than anyone else in the league, because he started so far behind that a good auction only got him to bad.

Nothing at the Expired Rookie Auction — {{f.team.0012.era_lots_won}} players, {{f.team.0012.era_spend}}. All {{f.league.era_pool_size}} players sold there, men whose rookie deals ran out without a second one, went to other owners.

At the Free Agent Auction he won {{f.team.0012.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0012.faa_spend}}, and two of them were quarterbacks. Jared Goff cost {{f.team.0012.top_buy_price}}, {{f.team.0012.top_buy_pct_of_spend}} of his auction spending, and Matthew Stafford cost nearly as much again. Between them those two took two-thirds of what he spent.

Measured against the money, it worked. He spent {{f.team.0012.faa_off_spend}} on offense at the Free Agent Auction, and for what that money bought he ranked {{f.team.0012.faa_off_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}; only Blake Bombers and C-Town Chivalry got more for their money. The fair caveat is that he brought the weakest offense in the league into the auction, with the quarterback slot empty, so almost any sensible buy was an upgrade.

The quarterback spending answered a real need — he arrived at the auction with nobody on his active roster who could start at quarterback, and superflex punishes that harder than any other gap. In context it is harder to love, because almost none of his money reached a receiver room that ranks {{f.team.0012.wr_rank|ord}}. Odell Beckham at the league minimum was his answer there, and he signed and released Beckham twice.

The value buys are real and worth naming. Travis Kelce at a small price is a Low-end TE1 and an upgrade on a bench player carrying nearly five times the salary. Rhamondre Stevenson has already started and produced. Andres Borregales, signed at the league minimum, scored on opening night.
He spent {{f.team.0012.idp_auction_spend}} on defenders across both auctions, the least of any owner.

t.0012.faa_value.title: Who got the most for his money

captions.t.0012.faa_value: Ranked by how much each owner's starting offense improved between the auction lock and the close, for every dollar he spent on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends at the Free Agent Auction.

paragraphs: {{f.team.0012.contracts_count}} contract moves, {{f.team.0012.trades_count}} trade, {{f.team.0012.roster_removals_total}} removals, {{f.team.0012.cuts_penalty_2026}} charged this season and {{f.team.0012.cuts_penalty_2027_deferred}} deferred to next.

The contract sheet is all auction conversion: Goff, Stafford, Stevenson, Rachaad White, DeMarvion Overshown and Borregales all moved onto multi-year deals, and only Borregales is at the league minimum.
The single trade is small and good: a 2027 fourth to Real Deal Creel for George Karlaftis, now a starter on his defensive line, and a 2027 fifth.
Marquise Brown was the only real cut, carrying a penalty deferred to next season. The rest is {{f.team.0012.inyear_flyers}} in-year flyers, two of them the same player.

The rookie class is his best asset and the reason not to write him off. {{f.team.0012.rookie_picks_count}} picks, led by Carnell Tate at 1.02, a slot that has produced a usable player half the time, who is already starting as a Low-end WR3. Makai Lemon at 1.06 and Kaelon Black at 2.02 came from slots that have produced a usable player just under a third of the time, and both grade replacement-level so far; Ja'Kobi Lane at 3.02 and Drew Allar at 3.05 came from slots that almost never have. Two defenders at 4.02 and 6.12 have yet to play an NFL season.

He is {{f.team.0012.division_rank|ord}} of {{f.team.0012.division_size}}, behind C-Town Chivalry and Cleon Ca$h, and he plays each of them five times. C-Town is the best team in the league and Cleon Ca$h is fourth. Ten of his matchups this season come against those two, which is the worst divisional draw of anybody.

Strongest team in the league? No — {{f.team.0012.composite_rank}} of {{f.league.teams}}, last, with the most holes and the worst receiver room. Best offseason? Also no, but he is not the worst either, and the distinction matters: he brought the weakest offense in the league into the auction and nearly doubled it, filled a quarterback slot that had been empty since spring, and did it while still holding {{f.team.0012.cap_current_room}} of room — more than any other owner in the league. He is last, and he is last with money and a first-round rookie already starting.

His biggest advantage is the Stafford-Goff pair, in a quarterback room that ranks {{f.team.0012.qb_rank|ord}}. The biggest weakness is receiver, ranked {{f.team.0012.wr_rank|ord}}, where Mike Evans, a Mid WR3, is the best he has; his thin defense is the cheapest problem in the league to fix.

And then the strangest early result in the league. When this was written only {{f.league.wk_teams_final}} NFL teams had played, and the last-ranked roster has the second-best haul of anybody: {{f.team.0012.wk_points_final}} points from three finished starters. Rhamondre Stevenson led it, with a minimum-salary kicker and a minimum-salary cornerback behind him. Nothing about one night predicts a season, and his two expensive quarterbacks had not played yet.
